messages.subject: Truncated normal distribution problem
parts:
Hi

I am having a problem sampling from a truncated normal distribution.

In the dataset the lengths are rounded down to the nearest 10. To counter this I am trying to sample from a truncated normal distribution to find a better approximation of the actual lengths of the fish. However, I keep getting this error message:

SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'test' NOW (CHAIN 1).

  [1] "Rejecting initial value:"                                                                            

  [2] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."                                       

  [3] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value." 

 

I believe the problem is caused by the truncation as when I remove the truncation “T(L[i],U[i])” the model runs fine. I think that the model is sampling from the normal distribution and then comparing it to the truncation and disregarding it if it falls outside the truncation, which would set the log probability to 0 and crash the model.

Is there a fix to this or a better way to sample from the truncated normal distribution?

Thanks

Alan

Here is the stan code:

data{
  int <lower=0> N;
  //length
  real l[N];
}

transformed data{
  real<lower=0> L[N];
  real<lower=0> U[N];
  for (i in 1:N){
    L[i] = l[i]-1;
    U[i] = l[i]+10;
  }
}

parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigmasq;
  real mu;
  real l_p[N];
}

transformed parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  sigma = sqrt(sigmasq);
}

model{
  sigmasq~inv_gamma(0.001,0.001);
  //do a truncated normal
  for (i in 1:N){
      l_p[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[U[i],L[i]];  
  }
}

Here is the R-code I use to call it:

dat2<-dat[-which(dat$Age==-9),] 
plaice_data3 <- list(t=as.numeric(dat2[,1]), w=as.numeric(dat2[,2]), l=as.numeric(dat2[,3]), N=length(dat2$Age))
fit <- stan(file = 'test.stan', data = plaice_data3, iter = 2000, chains = 1)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Truncated normal distribution problem
parts:
Your parameter declarations are inconsistent with your
model. In general, every value of the parameters
that satisfies the declared constraints should have
support in the model.

So this parameter:

> real l_p[N];

is inconsistent with this sampling statement:

And shouldn't that be T[L[i], U[i]] if that's
lower and upper bounds?

because l_p[i] isn't constrained, but it onlyhas support
in the model in (U[i], L[i]).

So you really need to transform and apply a Jacobian,
because we don't yet allow varying constraints.

So you can declare

parameters {
vector[N] l_p_raw;

and then have transformed parameters (assuming U[i] is
upper bound and L[i] lower bound:

transformed parameters {
vector[N] l_p;
for (n in 1:N)
l_p[n] = (U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + U[n];

model {
target += log((U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) * (1 - inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]));

That's not the most efficient way to implement things, but it should
work if values aren't too extreme. Otherwise you want
to use

target+= log(U[n] - L[n]) + log_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + log1m_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]);

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Truncated normal distribution problem
parts:
On another note, you can avoid declaring the variance as a transformed parameter and directly put a prior on sigma. That's usually advisable for several reasons. It avoids unnecessary computation (that's just a tiny benefit here) but more importantly sd is in the same units as y and so it's often easier to conceptualize what the prior on sigma implies. We also don't recommend those inverse-gamma priors as they are advertised as non-informative but really aren't. There's more on that topic in the manual and in Andrew's 2006 paper (cited in the manual).

Jonah
